opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea is that you don't want to be in a position where you discover a model is dangerous only after you've already trained it and maybe even deployed it. The whole policy is built around the notion that you should know *in advance* what safety measures you'll need, and have them ready before the capability shows up.

The way we try to build in that time is with a buffer. We define these AI Safety Levels, ASLs, which are tied to specific dangerous capabilities, things like meaningfully helping someone build a bioweapon, or being able to autonomously replicate and acquire resources. But we don't set our evaluations to trigger exactly at the point where a model has that capability. We design them to trigger somewhat earlier, at a kind of warning sign or "yellow line." If a model passes those evals, it doesn't necessarily mean it's dangerous yet. It means it's getting close enough that we need to have the next level of safeguards in place before we keep going.

Part of that buffer is about how often we test. Training runs scale up continuously, so we commit to running evaluations at regular intervals, in terms of effective compute, and also periodically during training. The concern is that capabilities can jump between checks, so the margin has to be big enough that even if you get a surprising jump between one evaluation and the next, you haven't blown past the actual danger threshold without noticing.

Then there's the organizational side of preparing. The policy forces us to think about the next ASL's safeguards, the security and deployment measures, while we're still at the current level. If we hit the trigger and those safeguards aren't ready, the commitment is that we pause scaling or deployment until they are. That creates a strong incentive to do the preparation work early, because nobody wants to be the reason the company has to stop. In a lot of ways that's the most important mechanism. It turns safety from something you do reactively into something that's on the critical path of the research roadmap.

I'll be honest that none of this is perfect. Evaluations are hard to get right, there's a real risk of underestimating what a model can do, especially once people figure out better ways to prompt or scaffold it, and we've had to keep revising the policy as we learn. But the basic principle, test early, leave margin, and have the protections ready before you need them, is, I think, the right way to approach it.

r001.rationale: The response says preparation becomes part of the research roadmap and creates an incentive to prepare early, but does not explain that this happens by aligning safety goals with commercial goals.

r002.rationale: It says evaluations trigger at a warning sign before the dangerous capability threshold, giving time to put the next level of safeguards in place.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core idea behind the RSP is that you don't want to be in a position where you discover a model is dangerous and you have to figure out, right then, what to do about it. That's the worst possible time to be making those decisions, because there's commercial pressure, there's time pressure, and you haven't done the thinking in advance.

So the way the policy is structured is that we define these AI Safety Levels, ASLs, and for each level we try to specify two things ahead of time. One is the capability threshold, the thing the model would have to be able to do for us to say, "Okay, this is now in the next tier of risk." And the other is the set of safeguards, the security measures and deployment measures, that we commit to having in place before we train or deploy a model at that level.

The key mechanism for buying time is the evaluations. We're not just testing the frontier model we're about to ship. We're trying to test for capabilities with a buffer, so we're asking whether the model is getting close to the threshold, not whether it's crossed it. And we commit to running those evaluations at regular intervals during training, every certain amount of effective compute, so that we're not surprised by a big jump between checkpoints.

If an evaluation trips, that's when the policy kicks in. We can't just keep scaling. We either have to have the next level of safeguards ready, or we pause until we do. And the thing I find valuable about that is it turns a vague intention, "we'll be careful," into something concrete that you can be held to. Someone internally can point to the document and say, "This triggered, here's what we said we'd do."

I'll be honest that there's a lot of uncertainty in all of this. The hard part is that predicting when a capability shows up is genuinely difficult, and the evals are imperfect. So the buffer is doing a lot of work. You want the trigger to go off early enough that you have months to build the security and the mitigations, not weeks. And we've tried to be conservative there, but I think it's fair to say we're still learning how well that works in practice. The goal is really to shift the work of preparing earlier in time, so that by the time the dangerous capabilities actually arrive, the hard decisions have mostly already been made.

r001.rationale: The response says advance planning can reduce decision-making under commercial pressure, but does not explain that aligning safety goals with commercial goals makes preparation part of ordinary company planning.

r002.rationale: The response says evaluations use a buffer to detect when a model is getting close to the threshold, with triggers intended to provide months for safeguards and mitigations before dangerous capabilities arrive.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish the point where a capability becomes dangerous from the point where you need to start preparing for it. If you wait until you’ve demonstrated the dangerous capability, you may already be too late to build and test the safeguards you need.

So you want an earlier warning threshold, with enough margin to account for how quickly capabilities might improve and how long the mitigations will take. Crossing that threshold should trigger concrete preparation: developing evaluations, improving security, and testing whether your safeguards actually work. Then, before you cross the dangerous capability threshold, those safeguards need to be in place.

The difficult part is that we don’t know precisely where those thresholds are, and our evaluations can miss things. So the policy needs to account for that uncertainty. And it needs a credible commitment to pause if capabilities advance faster than your ability to manage the risks. Otherwise, the preparation deadline is just an aspiration.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety preparation and company commitments but does not connect safety goals with commercial goals or say that preparation becomes part of ordinary company planning.

r002.rationale: It describes an earlier warning threshold with enough margin before dangerous capabilities, whose crossing triggers preparation so safeguards can be ready beforehand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you need to act before you actually observe the dangerous capability. If you wait until a model clearly has it, and only then start figuring out the safeguards, you may have left yourself very little time.

So I’d want the policy to distinguish between the threshold where particular safeguards must be in place and an earlier point where you start preparing them. You work backwards: how long would it take to develop and test the relevant security measures, or to establish that your deployment safeguards actually work? Then you need enough warning to do that work, with some margin for being wrong.

Evaluations are part of that, but they’re not a perfect forecasting tool. You also need to consider what the next training run might produce, rather than just what the current model can do. And if you reach the capability threshold before the safeguards are ready, the commitment to stop has to be real. Otherwise, the preparation deadline is just an aspiration.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preparing safeguards early, but does not connect safety goals with commercial goals or say that preparation becomes part of ordinary company planning.

r002.rationale: The response mentions evaluations and an earlier preparation point, but does not identify RSP yellow-line evaluations or state that they are designed to trigger before dangerous red-line capabilities.
